title: Abominations in the Temple
summary: While the elders of Judah sit in his house in Babylon, Ezekiel is carried in a vision to the temple in Jerusalem. A divine guide shows him four scenes, each worse than the last: an idol at the north gate, seventy elders burning incense before engraved images in a hidden room, women weeping for the god Tammuz, and twenty-five men with their backs to the temple bowing to the sun. God declares that he will respond in wrath and will not listen to their cries.
story: Chapters 8 to 11 form one long vision, the second of Ezekiel's great visions after his call in chapters 1 to 3. The first seven chapters announced that Jerusalem would fall. This vision shows why, and it shows something even more alarming: the presence of God is about to leave his own house. Chapter 8 is the evidence. The prophet is led deeper and deeper into the temple complex, and at every step he is told, “you will see even greater abominations.” In the chapters that follow, executioners are sent through the city (chapter 9), fire is scattered over it (chapter 10), and the glory of the LORD departs (chapters 10 and 11). The vision reverses in chapter 43, when Ezekiel sees the glory return to a new temple.
historical:
The vision is dated to the sixth year of King Jehoiachin's exile, on the fifth day of the sixth month, which corresponds to late summer or early autumn of 592 BC. Jerusalem was still standing under Zedekiah, the king the Babylonians had placed on the throne. The elders sitting in Ezekiel's house were leaders of the exiled community, who apparently came to him for a word from God (compare 14:1 and 20:1).

The vision names one man: Jaazaniah son of Shaphan (verse 11). A royal official named Shaphan served King Josiah as secretary and brought him the book of the law found in the temple (2 Kings 22), and several of Shaphan's sons later protected the prophet Jeremiah. If this Jaazaniah belonged to that family, as many scholars think, the scene is especially bitter: a son of the reforming secretary leads the elders in secret idolatry. The text does not say so directly, and Shaphan was not a rare name, so the identification is likely but not certain.
cultural:
Each scene reflects a real form of ancient worship. The engraved “crawling creature and detestable beast” (verse 10) suggest animal imagery of the kind found in Egyptian religion and elsewhere, and the secret room with censers suggests a private cult among the ruling class. Tammuz (verse 14) was a Mesopotamian god, known in Sumerian as Dumuzi, a shepherd figure whose death and descent to the underworld were mourned in ritual lament; a month in the Babylonian calendar, which later became a month in the Jewish calendar, bears his name. Women weeping for him at the temple gate were joining a foreign mourning rite inside the LORD's house. Sun worship (verse 16) was widespread in the ancient Near East, and 2 Kings 23:11 reports that Josiah removed horses and chariots dedicated to the sun from the temple entrance a generation earlier.

The position of the twenty-five men matters. The temple faced east, so worshipers facing the sanctuary faced west. These men turned their backs on the temple of the LORD to bow toward the rising sun, a posture that says in body language what their worship says in substance. The meaning of “putting the branch to their nose” (verse 17) is unknown. Suggestions include a ritual gesture with a plant, an obscene gesture, or an insult; Jewish scribal tradition also lists this verse among places where scribes are said to have softened an original reading that referred to God's own nose. No explanation has won general agreement.
literary: The chapter is built like a guided tour with rising intensity. Four times the guide shows the prophet a scene, and after the first three he says there are “greater abominations” still to come (verses 6, 13, 15). The route moves physically inward, from the outer north gate, through a hole dug in a wall, to the gate of the house of the LORD, and finally into the inner court between the portico and the altar, the holiest area a layperson could approach. The closer the prophet gets to the center, the worse the sin. The repeated question “Son of man, do you see?” draws the reader into the prophet's position as a witness. The chapter also sets up the next: the elders' claim that “The LORD does not see us” (verse 12) is answered by a vision in which God sees everything.

outline.t: Carried by the Spirit from Babylon to Jerusalem
The idol of jealousy at the north gate
Seventy elders burning incense in a hidden room
Twenty-five men bowing to the sun, and God's answer

doctrines.note: The chapter shows idolatry at the center of Israel's religious life, practiced by elders, women, and men in the very courts of the temple. Idolatry is not only something done by outsiders; it can flourish inside the house of God among those who lead it.

God says these practices “drive Me far from My sanctuary” (verse 6). His presence is holy, and a sanctuary filled with other gods is no longer a place where he will stay. This prepares for the departure of his glory in chapters 10 and 11.
The elders believe “The LORD does not see us” (verse 12). The whole vision answers them: God sees what is done in the dark and in secret rooms. His knowledge of human hearts and actions is complete.

words.note: Kavod, glory. The word's root carries the idea of weight or heaviness, and it came to mean honor, splendor, and the visible, radiant presence of God. Ezekiel saw this glory by the Kebar canal in chapter 1, and now sees it in the temple (verse 4). The coming chapters trace its movement out of the temple and, much later, its return.

Qin'ah, jealousy. The idol at the north gate is called the idol “that provokes jealousy” (verse 3). God's jealousy is his exclusive claim on his people's worship, like a spouse's rightful claim on faithfulness. The image set up in his house provokes that claim directly.

Tammuz, the Mesopotamian god known in Sumerian as Dumuzi. This is the only place in the Bible where he is named. His presence shows how far foreign religion had penetrated Jerusalem, even into rites performed at the temple gates.

Shemesh, sun. The men in verse 16 bow to it, facing east. Genesis 1 had refused even to name the sun, calling it the greater light, and the Law forbade worship of the sun, moon, and stars (Deuteronomy 4:19). Here the creature is worshiped in the Creator's own courts.

christ: The vision's central concern, whether God's presence will remain with his people, runs straight to Jesus. John's Gospel says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and that we have seen his glory (John 1:14), using the language of God's presence in the tabernacle and temple. Jesus cleared the temple courts of trade (John 2:13-22) and spoke of his own body as the temple. The connection is thematic: Ezekiel sees the glory about to depart from a defiled temple, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the place where God's glory comes to dwell again among his people, and then, through the Spirit, in them (1 Corinthians 3:16).

hard.q: How could religious leaders practice idolatry inside the temple and still think of themselves as faithful?
hard.a: The text gives a clue in verse 12: the elders believed that the LORD did not see them and had forsaken the land. After the deportation of 597 BC, many in Jerusalem may have concluded that the God of Israel had failed or withdrawn, and so they turned to other powers for help, while keeping the outward forms of temple life. Ancient religion was also generally inclusive; adding one more god to a household or a shrine did not feel like betrayal to most people in the ancient world. What the prophets insisted on was that the LORD is not one god among many but the only God, and that his covenant with Israel was exclusive. The chapter's point is that religious practice can continue at full volume while real trust has moved somewhere else.

questions: The elders did in a hidden room what they would not do in public. What does it mean to you that God sees what is done in the dark?
The men in verse 16 turned their backs on the temple to face the sun. What do you turn toward when you are anxious or afraid?
Each scene was “greater” than the last as the prophet moved closer to the center. Why do you think the worst corruption was found nearest the holy place?
